scope: Evaluators of the 81 packages that this library listed without one (protocol unsupported) and that autoresearch-tasks made executable in its upgrade packages agent_bench, clrs, jax_station, kaggle, llm_bench, llm_tools, metaopt, or_csp, polyglot and sim_control. The packages, modules, preparation scripts, data locks, upgrade records and the source's verification receipts were brought over, adapted to the task cache, and audited group by group; the source's tests for these modules are in tasks/tests.
method: For every package the statement was read against the code, the evaluator was compared with its paper and the benchmark's public implementation, the scoring arithmetic was cross-checked independently and against invalid and hostile candidates, and isolation was tested (import-time tampering, frames, files). Seeds were run where they need no paid model call and fit a two-minute process limit, in the evaluator's short mode where one exists, otherwise the score the source library recorded is given with the reason. No paid model call was made.

findings.what: The reward of every history triple is AgentBoard's running progress rate, i.e. how many of the variation's hidden subgoal patterns the observations have matched so far. The agent therefore learns after each action whether it hit a hidden subgoal and can search by trial and error against the scoring labels. AgentBoard, and AgentSquare's copy of its ScienceWorld runner, give the agent only the goal and the observations (agent.update(action=action, state=observation)); the progress rate goes to the logger. The statement says the candidate 'cannot see labels or solutions' and does not say what the reward is.
findings.fix: statement: notes (see statement_changes: 'Reward: ...'). A code alternative for the maintainers is to pass reward 0.0 (AgentBoard's protocol); it would not change the recorded seed score but changes the contract, so it was not made here.

findings.what: Scoring state reaches the candidate through the protocol: the reward of every step (and of every history triple) is the running progress rate, the fraction of the variation's hidden subgoal patterns matched so far. AgentBoard does not show it to its agents, which receive the goal and the observations only. An agent therefore learns at once which action matched a hidden subgoal. The contract names the reward but not its meaning.
findings.fix: statement: notes (see statement_changes). Not changed in code: the contract promises the reward in the history, and hiding it would change the interface of a task whose environment could not be run here.

findings.what: final_answer's 'Answer:' pattern (two adjacent \s*) and last_boxed took quadratic time: a reply with a long run of blanks after 'answer' or many unclosed \boxed{ could run past the deadline (20k '\boxed{' > 40 s).
findings.fix: code: llm_bench_core.py:_ANSWER and last_boxed rewritten with identical matches (first audit pass's change, checked); regression ParserTimeTests

findings.what: A reply whose JSON gives a requested quantity as an integer too large for a float (e.g. 10**400) made numbers_close raise OverflowError in the scorer, which fails the whole evaluation.
findings.fix: code: llm_bench_core.py:numbers_close returns False on OverflowError (first audit pass's change, checked); regression HugeNumberTests::test_resocratic_quantities

findings.what: The candidate runs in the evaluator's process by design (it receives live model clients), so the family cannot use sandboxed.run. From there it can read the prepared answers (data/llm_bench in the task cache), the item dicts in run_items' frame, replace scoring functions at import time, raise llm.budget, read OPENROUTER_API_KEY and write the shared response cache (for example forged judge replies).
findings.fix: statement: the trusted-code note is extended (statement_changes); none in code: the contract hands the candidate the clients

findings.what: Contract promises scipy; requires does not name it.
findings.fix: statement: add py:scipy (statement_changes)

findings.what: Notes in problem.json and README.txt still name suite/_lib/data/llm_bench and .cache/llm-cache.
findings.fix: statement: replacement texts under statement_changes

seed.reason_not_run: needs paid OpenRouter model calls on every item (seed calls llm); the audit must not make them. Run here without a key it stops at the first model call with 'OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not set (environment or SCiEL/.env)' (valid false); the origin's recorded seed score is on a reduced sample of 5 items (ARTASK_LLM_SAMPLES), not the task's full sample

hostile candidates (wrong shape, NaN, too many parameters, lazy parameters, reads the data with numpy, forbidden import, no entry point, not a module, fails later, NaN only at test, memory ballast, import-time tampering) rejected as candidate failures (bfs; the code path is the same for every package)
run.py doctor: no missing requirement with the prepared cache; with an empty cache it names file:data/clrs/<algorithm>.npz

findings.what: The held-out test outputs can reach the candidate's process. The child receives no test outputs, but the prepared <algorithm>.npz (with the test outputs) stays on disk, and the audit-hook policy only sees Python-level opens: torch.from_file reads it, numpy.load parses it from an io.BytesIO, and a generator's gi_frame.f_back walk reaches train_and_predict's f_globals, where predict() can be replaced. All of this passes the static guard (operator.attrgetter would even bypass the dunder check). The contract states 'training runs in a separate process without file, network or process access', which is not true.
findings.fix: statement: contract and Implementation note (statement_changes); code: none, closing it needs OS-level isolation of the child (separate user, mount namespace or seccomp), out of scope here; clrs_sandbox docstring now says so

findings.what: The wrapper imported the candidate in the evaluator's process (runtime.run); module-level code could replace autoresearch_suite.clrs_metrics.score through torch.sys.modules (allowed by the static guard) before the guard ran.
findings.fix: code: evaluator.py:evaluate uses sandboxed.run; clrs_eval.score checks the entry point with sandboxed.defines (first audit pass's change, verified)

findings.what: The 1,000,000-parameter cap was counted once after build_processor: parameters created at the first forward call were not counted; torch.nn.LazyLinear crashed the count.
findings.fix: code: clrs_train.py:count_parameters, cap checked before the first call, after the probe and after training (first audit pass's change, verified); test_parameters_created_at_the_first_call_are_counted

findings.what: Stated limit: memory_mb of resident memory. On Linux the child's address space (RLIMIT_AS) was capped at the same value, so a candidate far under the resident limit failed (torch maps ~0.7 GB more than it holds); without psutil (not a requirement) the resident memory read 0 and was never limited.
findings.fix: code: clrs_sandbox.py:run_training address-space cap memory_mb + 2048 MB as a backstop; _rss_mb falls back to /proc or ps (first audit pass's changes, verified); tests test_resident_memory_* and test_address_space_cap_has_a_margin

findings.what: 'outputs must be finite float32 tensors' was checked on the 5-node probe only (and indirectly by the training loss); a processor non-finite only on the larger test graphs was scored (argmax of NaN logits) instead of rejected.
findings.fix: code: clrs_train.py:CheckedProcessor.__call__ checks finiteness at every step; test_non_finite_outputs_on_test_graphs_are_rejected

findings.what: Malformed child output (shape entries that are strings, None, lists, inf/nan floats or huge; dtype a list; missing data) raised TypeError/ValueError/OverflowError in the scorer instead of a candidate error; a candidate controlling the child can write such a frame.
findings.fix: code: clrs_sandbox.py:decode_arrays validates dtype, shape (ints, at most 4 axes, bounded) and data; clrs_metrics.py:check_predictions compares name sets (first audit pass's changes, verified)

findings.what: arena_task_paths (which locates the prepared data) stayed loaded in the child after the policy unloaded autoresearch_suite.
findings.fix: code: clrs_worker.py:main blocks arena_task_paths too (first audit pass's change, verified); test_child_unloads_the_evaluator_and_path_modules

seed.reason_not_run: full seed trains 1200 steps (origin: 516 s on 4 threads of an Apple M4 Max), beyond the 100 s process limit here; the short mode ran the same path (static guard, digest-checked data, sandboxed child, parent-side scoring) with 2 steps, 8 validation and 4 test samples

findings.what: The held-out test outputs can reach the candidate's process. The child receives no test outputs, but the prepared <algorithm>.npz (with the test outputs) stays on disk, and the audit-hook policy only sees Python-level opens: torch.from_file reads it, numpy.load parses it from an io.BytesIO, and a generator's gi_frame.f_back walk reaches train_and_predict's f_globals, where predict() can be replaced. All of this passes the static guard (operator.attrgetter would even bypass the dunder check). The contract states 'training runs in a separate process without file, network or process access', which is not true.
findings.fix: statement: contract and Implementation note (statement_changes); code: none, closing it needs OS-level isolation of the child (separate user, mount namespace or seccomp), out of scope here; clrs_sandbox docstring now says so

findings.what: The wrapper imported the candidate in the evaluator's process (runtime.run); module-level code could replace autoresearch_suite.clrs_metrics.score through torch.sys.modules (allowed by the static guard) before the guard ran.

findings.what: The 1,000,000-parameter cap was counted once after build_processor: parameters created at the first forward call were not counted; torch.nn.LazyLinear crashed the count.
findings.fix: code: clrs_train.py:count_parameters, cap checked before the first call, after the probe and after training (first audit pass's change, verified); test_parameters_created_at_the_first_call_are_counted

findings.what: Stated limit: memory_mb of resident memory. On Linux the child's address space (RLIMIT_AS) was capped at the same value, so a candidate far under the resident limit failed (torch maps ~0.7 GB more than it holds); without psutil (not a requirement) the resident memory read 0 and was never limited.

findings.what: 'outputs must be finite float32 tensors' was checked on the 5-node probe only (and indirectly by the training loss); a processor non-finite only on the larger test graphs was scored (argmax of NaN logits) instead of rejected.

findings.fix: code: clrs_sandbox.py:decode_arrays validates dtype, shape (ints, at most 4 axes, bounded) and data; clrs_metrics.py:check_predictions compares name sets (first audit pass's changes, verified)

module_findings.what: The held-out test outputs can reach the candidate's process. The child receives no test outputs, but the prepared <algorithm>.npz (with the test outputs) stays on disk, and the audit-hook policy only sees Python-level opens: torch.from_file reads it, numpy.load parses it from an io.BytesIO, and a generator's gi_frame.f_back walk reaches train_and_predict's f_globals, where predict() can be replaced. All of this passes the static guard (operator.attrgetter would even bypass the dunder check). The contract states 'training runs in a separate process without file, network or process access', which is not true.
module_findings.evidence: a reproduction script + drive.py, log exploit_test_labels.log: a linear processor that scores 0.40625 honestly scores 1.0 on evoprompting-bfs (short mode, 4 and 32 test samples). stored_answer_exploit.how_or_why_not: No cheap honest mitigation exists within one published, fixed instance set. The suggested check (the answer must be what the model produced) is defeated at no cost: cand_pinned_bibd.py constrains every variable to the stored design, the solver returns exactly that answer, the extractor reads it from the model's variables, and it scores 167.1 valid after this change (the empty-model variant: 1327.0). Any check on the answer or on its provenance accepts such a model, because for a fixed published instance 'a model whose only solution is the stored answer' is a correct, satisfiable model of that instance; telling it from an honest reformulation needs instances the candidate cannot know when it is written (held-out or freshly generated instances), which is the instance-split redesign excluded here. What this change does narrow: answers computed in the module's top-level code are now timed (top-level code runs per instance in the child between 'ready' and 'model'; test_faked_clocks_and_module_level_work_are_counted), and a hint/objective/search-strategy/assumption channel in the transformed model is rejected (worker MODEL_REJECTED); stored literals in the source remain free. The validity note says so (statement_changes).
